item.title: Build to Rent pipeline dries up as starts drop sharply
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Build to Rent (BTR) sector is facing a significant downturn, with new developments starting on site plummeting by 79% across the UK in the year to June, according to recent research by Savills for Real Estate:UK (RE:UK). This sharp decline marks one of the steepest drops ever recorded in the sector, with regional areas outside London experiencing an even more pronounced fall of 84%. The slowdown is also impacting construction activity, as the number of BTR homes under construction fell by 21% nationwide in the second quarter compared to the previous year.

Challenges in the Build to Rent Sector

The decline in new BTR developments is part of a broader trend described by RE:UK as “pipeline exhaustion”. For the tenth consecutive quarter, completions have outpaced new starts, highlighting a growing imbalance in the sector. Whilst more schemes are securing planning permission, fewer are progressing to construction. This stagnation is largely attributed to mounting viability pressures, with developers facing higher costs and tougher market conditions.

Investors are increasingly favouring completed or operational BTR assets over funding new developments, further exacerbating the issue. Political uncertainty is also playing a role, with concerns over potential rent freezes and controls discouraging investment. A survey conducted by RE:UK found that all respondents would reduce investment in BTR schemes and avoid mayoral areas if rent controls were introduced. This uncertainty is prompting calls for greater policy clarity to support the sector’s growth.

The Impact on Housing Supply

Despite the slowdown, the BTR sector remains a key contributor to the UK’s housing supply, accounting for around 8% of all new homes completed nationwide. This underscores both the importance of the sector and the broader challenges affecting housing development. Danny Pinder, Director of RE:UK, commented on the findings, stating: “The Q2 2026 delivery figures have shown one of the sharpest declines in the number of new start-on-sites yet, and undoubtedly reflect the impact the viability crisis is having on the development of BTR schemes across the UK.”

Pinder also noted that the sharpest decline in starts occurred in regional areas, reflecting the difficulty of bringing forward new schemes despite strong underlying tenant demand. The combination of financial viability issues and increased regulatory uncertainty is creating a challenging environment for developers and investors alike.

The BTR sector’s struggles highlight the need for greater policy support and stability to ensure continued growth and contribution to the UK’s housing market. Without intervention, the delivery of new rental homes could be further restricted, exacerbating the existing housing shortage.

item.title: House price growth slows to 1.8% in July
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK house prices rose by 1.8% annually in July, marking a continued slowdown in growth compared to previous months. While the market shows signs of cooling, industry observers note that determined buyers can still find opportunities in what remains a fundamentally stable housing landscape.

Understanding the slowdown

The latest figures represent the lowest annual price increase since early 2023, with several factors contributing to the moderation:

  • Higher mortgage rates affecting buyer affordability
  • Ongoing economic uncertainty influencing purchasing decisions
  • A gradual rebalancing between supply and demand

Regional variations continue to play a significant role, with some areas experiencing more pronounced slowdowns than others. The South of England has seen particularly marked deceleration, while more affordable regions maintain relatively stronger growth.

Opportunities for buyers

Despite the cooling market, property professionals highlight several positive aspects for those considering a purchase:

  • Reduced competition compared to the post-pandemic boom period
  • More realistic pricing from motivated sellers
  • Greater room for negotiation in many transactions

First-time buyers might find the current conditions particularly favourable, especially when combined with government support schemes. Meanwhile, homeowners looking to upsize could benefit from the narrowing gap between property tiers.

While the housing market continues to adjust to new economic realities, the underlying demand for quality homes remains robust. Prospective buyers may wish to research local market conditions thoroughly and seek independent mortgage advice to understand their options in the current climate.

item.title: Transaction uptick but autumn real test
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK property transactions showed modest growth in June, with a 2% annual increase according to the latest figures. However, industry analysts suggest the autumn property market may prove more revealing about the true state of buyer sentiment and housing market resilience.

Summer market shows cautious improvement

The slight uptick in residential transactions during June indicates some stability returning to the housing market after recent economic challenges. While the increase appears modest, it represents the first year-on-year growth in several months, potentially signalling the beginning of a gradual recovery phase.

Several factors may have contributed to this improvement:

  • Stabilisation of mortgage rates after previous volatility
  • Increased buyer confidence as inflation shows signs of easing
  • Seasonal demand patterns typical for summer months

Autumn market to reveal true picture

Property experts caution that the autumn period will provide more meaningful insights into market health. The traditional post-summer period often sees:

  • Increased market activity as families complete moves before school terms
  • More accurate reflection of buyer confidence levels
  • Clearer indications of pricing trends and demand patterns

Market observers will be watching several key indicators in the coming months, including mortgage approval rates, price adjustments, and the volume of new listings entering the market. These factors could help determine whether the June transaction increase represents the start of sustained recovery or merely a temporary seasonal fluctuation.

For those considering property transactions, the autumn period may offer valuable insights into market direction and potential opportunities. As always, consulting with independent mortgage advisers could help borrowers navigate the changing landscape.

item.title: NI house prices rise £9,000 since last year
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Northern Ireland's property market has seen consistent growth over the past year, with both house prices and rental costs increasing by 3.8% annually during the second quarter. This upward trend reflects an ongoing imbalance between housing demand and available supply across the region.

Sustained price growth in Northern Ireland

Property values in Northern Ireland have risen by approximately £9,000 compared to the same period last year, continuing a pattern of gradual appreciation. The regional market appears resilient despite broader economic uncertainties, with buyer competition remaining strong for limited housing stock. Industry observers note that this sustained demand, coupled with constrained supply, continues to put upward pressure on prices across all property types.

Rental market follows similar pattern

The rental sector mirrors the sales market's trajectory, with a matching 3.8% increase in average rents. This parallel growth suggests that affordability challenges affect both prospective buyers and tenants in Northern Ireland. Property professionals highlight that while the rate of increase remains moderate compared to some UK regions, the consistent upward movement warrants attention from both investors and those looking for accommodation.

Prospective buyers and renters might consider reviewing their budgets carefully against these market conditions. Homeowners contemplating selling could find favourable conditions, though local market variations mean obtaining several valuations from estate agents may prove worthwhile. As always, consulting with mortgage advisers about financing options remains essential in this evolving market landscape.

item.title: Major property firm launches £41.9m share buyback
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Taylor Wimpey has announced a £41.9 million share buyback scheme, with the programme commencing immediately and expected to complete before 31st December this year. The initiative forms part of the housebuilder’s capital management strategy and will see repurchased shares subsequently cancelled.

How the share buyback works

The FTSE 100 developer has engaged Merrill Lynch International to independently execute the share repurchases on its behalf. Transactions will occur on the London Stock Exchange under the authority granted at Taylor Wimpey’s 2026 Annual General Meeting, which permits the acquisition of up to 333.8 million ordinary shares. The £41.9 million figure excludes associated costs such as brokerage fees, stamp duty and other administrative expenses.

Share buybacks typically indicate a company’s confidence in its financial position, as the process reduces the number of shares in circulation – potentially increasing the value of remaining shares. Taylor Wimpey has confirmed all repurchases will comply with UK Market Abuse Regulations and Listing Rules, with the company pledging to provide regular updates throughout the buyback period.

Context for property market observers

This move follows similar announcements from other major UK property firms, including Rightmove’s recent £350 million buyback programme. For those monitoring the housing sector, such developments may signal how leading market participants view their future prospects amidst current economic conditions.

While share buybacks primarily affect investors rather than homebuyers, industry analysts often view them as indicators of corporate health. A robust housebuilding sector could potentially support sustained housing supply – an important factor for prospective purchasers considering market conditions.

Taylor Wimpey’s decision to return capital to shareholders through this mechanism comes as the property market demonstrates resilience despite broader economic challenges. Market watchers may wish to monitor forthcoming trading statements for insights into how the company’s strategy develops in coming months.

item.title: ‘Acute’ need for new homes – has Andy Burnham read Property Industry Eye?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK continues to face a severe housing shortage, with the government's target of delivering 1.5 million new homes before the next election appearing increasingly unrealistic. Industry experts suggest this ambitious goal may prove as challenging as completing a marathon in record time, given the current barriers facing developers. This shortfall has significant implications for the entire property market, not just new-build sales.

Why new homes matter to the wider market

While estate agents typically earn less from new-build sales than resales, the new homes market plays a crucial role in maintaining market fluidity. Consider the typical property chain: an older couple looking to downsize often requires a suitable new property to facilitate their move. Their existing home's sale may then enable multiple transactions further down the chain. Without sufficient new housing stock, these chains break down, potentially stagnating the entire market.

The challenges facing homebuilders

Developers currently face four major obstacles to increasing construction volumes:

  • Price pressures: Many areas have seen property price declines while land costs remain stubbornly high
  • Construction costs: Building expenses have risen dramatically, with the Home Builders Federation estimating a £76,000 increase per home since 2020
  • Regulatory burdens: Planning applications have become more complex and expensive, while environmental compliance adds significant costs
  • Safety requirements: Post-Grenfell fire regulations, including mandatory second staircases in high-rises, reduce developable space and profitability

This £76,000 per-home cost increase comprises numerous factors including higher landfill taxes, increased community infrastructure levies, material price rises, and elevated labour costs following minimum wage increases and National Insurance changes. The second staircase requirement alone can eliminate two flats per floor in high-rise developments, substantially reducing gross development values.

The affordable housing conundrum

Compounding these challenges, some developments must allocate up to 50% of units as affordable housing. While socially important, this requirement further squeezes developer margins at a time when profitability is already under pressure. With these combined financial pressures, many developers are scaling back projects rather than expanding them.

For prospective buyers and homeowners looking to move, this constrained supply suggests continued competition for available properties. Those considering new-build purchases might find it worthwhile to research developers' incentives and explore shared ownership schemes where available. The current market conditions highlight why housing supply remains one of the UK's most persistent economic challenges.

item.title: Section 21 deadline triggers surge in possession claims
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The abolition of Section 21 evictions has seen a surge in landlord possession claims, as property owners raced to meet the final court deadline. New data reveals that July witnessed a 28% year-on-year increase in possession instructions, marking one of the busiest periods for landlords in the past year. The rush was driven by the impending 31 July deadline, after which valid Section 21 notices could no longer be relied upon unless court proceedings had already commenced.

Landlords Scramble to Meet the Deadline

July’s spike in possession claims highlights the urgency felt by landlords as the deadline approached. According to Paul Shamplina, founder of Landlord Action, the firm experienced exceptionally high call volumes, with staff working extended hours to handle inquiries. Many landlords waited until the final days to seek advice or initiate claims, which added to the pressure. Shamplina emphasised that instructing a solicitor close to the deadline did not guarantee a successful claim, as any error in the notice or supporting paperwork could lead to rejection.

The transition away from Section 21 has created significant uncertainty for landlords. Those who missed the deadline must now rely on the revised Section 8 possession grounds, which came into effect on 1 May. These grounds require landlords to demonstrate specific reasons for seeking possession, such as rent arrears, selling the property, or intending to move in themselves. For landlords accustomed to the flexibility of Section 21, this represents a major shift in how they manage their properties.

Revised Section 8 Grounds in Focus

Early data from Landlord Action provides insights into how landlords are adapting to the new rules. In July, 39% of possession cases involved rent-related grounds, such as Grounds 8, 10, or 11, which address rent arrears or persistent delays in payment. Ground 1A, which allows landlords to regain possession when planning to sell the property, accounted for 30% of cases. Meanwhile, Ground 1, used when the landlord or a family member intends to occupy the property, featured in 8% of cases. A further 29% of claims fell under other grounds, reflecting the diverse circumstances landlords now face.

While meeting the deadline was a significant hurdle, landlords now face a new challenge: navigating a court system already under strain. With many courts understaffed and overwhelmed by existing caseloads, landlords may experience lengthy delays in processing, hearing, and enforcing possession claims. This could prolong the uncertainty for both landlords and tenants.

The shift away from Section 21 marks a new era in the UK rental market, with landlords needing to adapt to stricter regulations. For those who missed the deadline, understanding the revised Section 8 grounds and seeking professional advice could be essential steps in managing their properties effectively.

item.title: Ambitious agency completes second acquisition of the year
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Edinburgh's private rented sector has seen significant consolidation this year as Albany Lettings completes its second strategic acquisition of 2026. The property management firm has strengthened its market position by purchasing Hadden Rankin Property Management, a respected local business with over two decades of experience serving landlords and tenants across the Scottish capital.

Strategic Expansion in Edinburgh's Rental Market

This latest acquisition follows Albany's purchase of LinnMac Property and Investment Letting in March, demonstrating the company's ambitious growth strategy through targeted mergers. Hadden Rankin brings extensive expertise in lettings, compliance support and investment advice to the enlarged business. The deal is expected to expand Albany's management portfolio while maintaining service continuity for existing clients.

Michael Mairs, Albany's Scotland regional director, emphasised that growth must enhance customer experience rather than simply increase scale. The company aims to combine Hadden Rankin's trusted local reputation with Albany's broader operational resources, creating a more robust offering for Edinburgh's rental market.

Commitment to Service Continuity

Transition planning appears central to Albany's acquisition strategy. Mairs highlighted the importance of preserving Hadden Rankin's valuable client relationships and property knowledge during the handover process. The company stresses that landlords and tenants should notice minimal disruption, with the same personal service now supported by enhanced back-office capabilities.

Founders Ross Hadden and Dorothy Rankin expressed confidence in the transition, noting Albany's shared commitment to professional, localised property management. Their decision to sell was reportedly driven by securing long-term service quality for clients rather than purely financial considerations.

For landlords with properties under Hadden Rankin's management, this acquisition may bring access to broader resources whilst maintaining the personal service they value. Tenants might benefit from more streamlined processes while retaining their existing points of contact.

This deal continues the trend of consolidation in Scotland's property services sector, with established local firms joining larger groups to combine niche expertise with operational scale. As the private rented sector evolves, such strategic mergers could become increasingly common across UK regional markets.

item.title: Are property firms delivering real diversity and inclusion?
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property sector has long grappled with gender imbalance, particularly in leadership roles. Whilst progress has been made in recent years, industry observers question whether current diversity initiatives are tackling symptoms rather than root causes. The sector's historical male dominance creates a cyclical challenge – without visible female leaders, succession planning tends to perpetuate the status quo.

Confidence Gap Highlights Systemic Issues

Recent industry programmes designed to support women's advancement have revealed unexpected insights. Rather than focusing on overcoming unconscious bias – often assumed to be the primary barrier – many female participants identified confidence and assertiveness as their key development areas. This suggests women in property still feel they need permission to claim their space in an industry where male voices have traditionally dominated.

Such findings raise important questions about whether diversity initiatives should focus more on systemic change rather than preparing women to navigate male-dominated environments. Younger generations entering the sector appear more willing to challenge workplace norms, potentially driving cultural shifts from within.

Legislative Changes Offer Hope

The recently strengthened Employment Rights Act, with its sharper focus on workplace harassment, could prove transformative. Combined with evolving workplace cultures, these legal changes may help create environments where diverse talent can thrive. Early signs suggest this generational shift in attitudes could gradually reshape the property sector's leadership landscape.

However, meaningful progress requires more than just participation from women. When male leaders engage with diversity programmes, many report gaining new perspectives on the challenges female colleagues face. Some have gone on to initiate discussions within their own teams – a promising indicator of cultural change taking root.

The Road Ahead

Whilst mentoring and development schemes play an important role, true inclusion requires structural changes in recruitment, promotion and workplace culture. The property industry may need to consider more fundamental reforms to its talent pipelines and leadership development approaches to accelerate progress.

As the sector continues this evolution, measuring outcomes rather than just participation in diversity programmes will be crucial. The coming years may reveal whether current initiatives lead to genuine transformation or whether more radical approaches are needed to achieve meaningful gender balance in UK property.

This suggests women in property still feel they need permission to claim their space in an industry where male voices have traditionally dominated.

Such findings raise important questions about whether diversity initiatives should focus more on systemic change rather than preparing women to navigate male-dominated environments. Younger generations entering the sector appear more willing to challenge workplace norms, potentially driving cultural shifts from within.

Legislative Changes Offer Hope

The recently strengthened Employment Rights Act, with its sharper focus on workplace harassment, could prove transformative. Combined with evolving workplace cultures, these legal changes may help create environments where diverse talent can thrive. Early signs suggest this generational shift in attitudes could gradually reshape the property sector's leadership landscape.

However, meaningful progress requires more than just participation from women. When male leaders engage with diversity programmes, many report gaining new perspectives on the challenges female colleagues face. Some have gone on to initiate discussions within their own teams – a promising indicator of cultural change taking root.

The Road Ahead

Whilst mentoring and development schemes play an important role, true inclusion requires structural changes in recruitment, promotion and workplace culture. The property industry may need to consider more fundamental reforms to its talent pipelines and leadership development approaches to accelerate progress.

As the sector continues this evolution, measuring outcomes rather than just participation in diversity programmes will be crucial. The coming years may reveal whether current initiatives lead to genuine transformation or whether more radical approaches are needed to achieve meaningful gender balance in UK property.

item.title: Acquisition strengthens fast-growing operator
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

StayRight, a prominent player in the short-term rental sector, has significantly expanded its operations in South Wales through the acquisition of Cohost Partners. This marks one of the largest independent short-let management deals in the region, reinforcing StayRight’s position as a key operator in the serviced accommodation market.

Strategic Growth in the Short-Let Sector

The acquisition of Cohost Partners follows StayRight’s earlier purchase of Just Stay Wales, highlighting the company’s ambitious expansion strategy. Originally founded by Matthew Lowe and later joined by Fran Brazil, Cohost Partners had grown into one of South Wales’ leading short-term rental management businesses. By integrating Cohost’s portfolio, StayRight strengthens its regional footprint and bolsters its managed property offerings.

This move reflects a broader trend of consolidation in the short-let management sector, as operators seek to enhance their scale and regional coverage. With increasing demand for flexible accommodation options, mergers and acquisitions have become a common strategy for businesses looking to capitalise on the market’s growth.

Industry Perspectives on the Deal

Zac Ratcliffe, director of StayRight, described the acquisition as a natural step forward, given the companies’ existing competition in the market. He emphasised StayRight’s ambition to solidify its position as Wales’ largest independent management company, with further growth expected in the coming years.

The transaction was facilitated by Think Acquisition, a specialist in brokering deals within the serviced accommodation sector. Leon Gorman, director of Think Acquisition, noted the complexities involved in valuing and structuring such businesses, citing this as the firm’s fourth completed deal in the sector within a 12-month period. He expressed enthusiasm for continuing to support this dynamic and evolving industry.

For property investors and landlords, the consolidation of short-let management firms could mean more streamlined services and potentially greater opportunities for portfolio growth. As the market continues to evolve, staying informed about such developments may help stakeholders make well-considered decisions.

item.title: Mortgage Ready: Strengthening Your Application
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Securing a mortgage involves more than just demonstrating a stable income. Lenders assess how responsibly borrowers manage their finances over time, making it crucial to prepare well in advance. Fortunately, many factors influencing a mortgage application are within a homeowner’s control, and early planning can significantly improve the chances of securing a favourable deal.

Understanding Lender Criteria

Mortgage lenders evaluate applications based on several key factors, including credit history, affordability, and financial stability. A strong application typically reflects a consistent track record of managing debts, paying bills on time, and maintaining a healthy credit score. Borrowers might consider reviewing their credit report several months before applying to identify and address any potential issues, such as missed payments or errors.

Additionally, lenders often scrutinise bank statements to assess spending habits. Reducing unnecessary expenses and avoiding large, unexplained transactions could help present a more favourable financial profile. Keeping savings in a separate account might also demonstrate prudent money management.

Improving Affordability

Lenders use affordability calculations to determine how much borrowers can comfortably repay. This includes assessing income, outgoings, and existing debts. Homeowners may wish to pay down outstanding debts, such as credit cards or loans, to improve their debt-to-income ratio. Reducing monthly commitments, even slightly, could make a significant difference in the eyes of a lender.

Another way to enhance affordability is by increasing income, where possible. This might involve taking on additional work, securing a pay rise, or exploring other sources of earnings. Stable, long-term income streams are particularly valued by lenders.

Preparing Documentation

Having the right documentation ready can streamline the mortgage application process. Borrowers typically need to provide proof of identity, address, income, and outgoings. This may include payslips, bank statements, tax returns, and utility bills. Ensuring these documents are accurate, up to date, and easily accessible could save time and avoid delays.

For self-employed individuals or those with irregular income, lenders may require additional evidence, such as business accounts or accountant’s letters. Preparing these in advance might help strengthen the application and demonstrate financial reliability.

Taking proactive steps to strengthen a mortgage application could improve the likelihood of approval and secure better terms. By understanding lender criteria, improving affordability, and preparing documentation, borrowers can present a more compelling case to potential lenders. Early planning and attention to detail often make all the difference.

item.title: Tenants! The Renters’ Guide is live again and updated for the Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Private renters in England and Wales now have access to an updated version of The Renters' Guide, a comprehensive online resource designed to help tenants understand their rights under the new Renters' Rights Act. Originally launched in 2021 by legal expert Harriet Thomas, the revamped website offers practical guidance through an extensive question-and-answer format.

What Makes The Renters' Guide Different?

Unlike many tenant advice websites that present information in standard article format, The Renters' Guide takes an interactive approach. Visitors begin by typing their specific rental query into a prominent search box on the homepage. The system then surfaces relevant answers from a database containing hundreds of common tenant concerns.

The guide covers all aspects of private renting including:

  • Deposit protection schemes
  • Repairs and maintenance responsibilities
  • Rent increases and payment issues
  • Eviction processes and notice periods
  • New protections under the Renters' Rights Act

Keeping Up With Legislative Changes

The recent update incorporates changes introduced by the Renters' Rights Act, which came into force earlier this year. Tenants might find the refreshed content particularly useful for understanding:

  • New rules around no-fault evictions
  • Updated requirements for property standards
  • Changes to tenancy deposit dispute processes
  • Enhanced protections against unfair rental practices

With private renting becoming increasingly common across the UK, resources like The Renters' Guide could prove valuable for tenants navigating the complexities of the rental market. The question-led format allows renters to quickly find answers to specific concerns without wading through lengthy guides.

Whilst the website doesn't replace professional legal advice, it may serve as a helpful starting point for tenants seeking to understand their rights and responsibilities under current legislation.

item.title: Britain’s housing crisis is ‘entirely self-inflicted’, think tank warns
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s housing crisis has been described as “entirely self-inflicted” by a leading think tank, which argues that decades of underbuilding have stifled economic growth and exacerbated the nation’s housing shortage. The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) has released a report highlighting how restrictive planning rules and a lack of investment in infrastructure have created significant barriers to development, impacting not only housing but also commercial property and essential facilities.

Decades of Underbuilding

According to the IEA, the UK’s housing stock has grown at a much slower rate in recent decades compared to the 19th and early 20th centuries. Historically, housing stock expanded by 1% to 2% annually, but this figure has dropped to around 0.5% over the past 60 years. This slowdown has contributed to a severe shortage of homes, driving up prices and making housing increasingly unaffordable for many.

The report also challenges the notion that England is overdeveloped, noting that only around 10% of the country’s land is built on. Agricultural land still dominates, covering nearly two-thirds of the nation. The IEA argues that this highlights the potential for further development, provided planning policies are reformed to facilitate growth.

Impact on Economic Growth

The housing crisis extends beyond residential property, with a lack of commercial premises also hindering economic progress. The IEA warns that insufficient office spaces, laboratories, and infrastructure are driving up business costs, reducing productivity, and limiting expansion in key economic areas. This, in turn, has contributed to nearly two decades of stagnant real income growth in the UK.

Dr Kristian Niemietz, economist and author of the report, stated: “The British economy is rubbing up against physical capacity constraints. We are trying to squeeze a twenty-first-century economy into the physical built-up environment inherited from the previous two centuries, and we refuse to expand that capacity to the degree required.”

Policy Failures and the Path Forward

The IEA report criticises successive governments for failing to implement meaningful reforms despite recognising the issue for over two decades. While policy papers and reviews have acknowledged the problem, the think tank argues that decisive action has been lacking. The report forms part of the IEA’s broader series, The Great Stagnation, which examines the causes of the UK’s prolonged economic slowdown.

Lord Hannan, Director General of the IEA, emphasised the need for change, stating: “Every fast-growing economy in history has addressed its physical infrastructure constraints. Without significant reforms, the UK risks falling further behind.”

As the housing crisis continues to impact millions, the IEA’s findings underscore the urgent need for policy reforms to unlock development and stimulate economic growth. Homeowners, renters, and businesses alike may find themselves affected by these ongoing challenges, highlighting the importance of addressing the root causes of the UK’s housing shortage.

item.title: Latest figures strengthen case for homebuying reform
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent housing market data reveals steady buyer demand amidst ongoing challenges with transaction efficiency. While property sales showed modest monthly growth in June, industry experts argue that the homebuying process itself remains a significant barrier to market fluidity. With calls for reform growing louder, estate agents are urging policymakers to prioritise improvements to the current system.

Market Activity Shows Resilience

HM Revenue & Customs figures indicate 98,700 seasonally adjusted residential transactions in June – a slight increase from May's 98,460 and 2% higher than June 2023. This year-on-year growth is particularly notable given last year's spike in completions ahead of stamp duty changes. The data suggests underlying demand persists despite economic headwinds, with approximately 8% of English homeowners reportedly either planning to move or already in the process.

Nick Leeming of Jackson-Stops observes: "The market continues to move steadily, but this measured pace shouldn't be confused with lack of interest. Households are still motivated by employment, family needs and lifestyle changes, though they're taking longer to commit amid higher mortgage costs and economic uncertainty."

Reform Urged to Boost Market Efficiency

Industry leaders highlight how protracted transaction timelines continue to hamper market performance. Current estimates suggest streamlining the process could potentially unlock 260,000 additional home moves annually across England. Key areas for improvement include:

  • Increasing transaction speed and predictability
  • Enhancing transparency throughout the process
  • Reducing unnecessary administrative barriers

Leeming notes: "While no single change will revolutionise the market overnight, meaningful progress in these areas could provide greater confidence for participants. A more efficient system would benefit both buyers and sellers, supporting healthier market dynamics."

With affordability pressures and economic conditions likely to influence activity in coming months, optimising the transaction process represents one practical avenue for positive change. As the new government settles in, the property sector will be watching closely for signs of commitment to homebuying reform.

item.title: Rightmove’s AI bet is paying off
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Rightmove's strategic focus on artificial intelligence appears to be delivering tangible benefits, with recent half-year results showing improved consumer engagement and stronger lead generation for estate agents. The property portal's shares rose nearly 2% on Friday as investors reacted positively to financial performance that broadly matched expectations, despite ongoing challenges in the new homes market.

AI tools driving engagement

The portal's "Ask Rightmove" feature, powered by conversational AI technology, has emerged as a particular success story. Early data suggests this tool is helping prospective buyers and renters find properties more efficiently, while simultaneously delivering higher quality leads to partner agents. Alongside this innovation, Rightmove reports users are spending more time on its platform - a key metric that reinforces its dominant position in the UK's online property sector.

Anthony Codling of RBC Capital Markets noted: "Concrete evidence shows 'Ask Rightmove' is driving higher engagement and lead conversion. We continue to believe Rightmove is an AI winner." The company plans to introduce additional AI-powered features later this year, with a focus on further enhancing lead quality and streamlining agents' workflows.

Resilient performance in challenging market

Rightmove's results demonstrate notable resilience, with first-half revenue meeting forecasts and underlying operating profit slightly exceeding expectations. Much of this strength stems from the portal's core estate agency business, where high customer retention and ongoing product investment have helped counterbalance weaker conditions in the new-build sector.

Analysts highlighted that Rightmove's reduced full-year revenue guidance relates specifically to the new homes market rather than any fundamental demand issue in its primary agency business. The company's profit outlook remains unchanged, suggesting confidence in its ability to navigate current housing market uncertainties.

While some estate agents may question the portal's subscription fees during a challenging sales environment, Rightmove continues to invest in tools that extend user engagement. As one market observer noted, these product developments lay important foundations for future growth, regardless of broader housing market fluctuations.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, Rightmove's AI developments could mean more intuitive property searches and potentially faster connections with suitable agents. As the portal rolls out further innovations, its ability to maintain market leadership while adapting to changing consumer expectations will be one to watch.

item.title: UK rents gather pace as London pulls further ahead
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK rental prices maintained their upward trajectory in July, with London continuing to outpace other regions according to the latest HomeLet Rental Index. The data reveals a national average rent of £1,369 per month, marking a 1.2% monthly increase and 4.3% annual growth. The capital's rental market remains particularly buoyant, with prices reaching £2,207 on average – 6% higher than the same period last year.

Regional rental trends across the UK

Eleven of twelve monitored regions recorded monthly rent increases in July, demonstrating widespread market strength. Scotland led monthly gains with a 2.6% rise, followed by the South East at 1.4%. The North East and North West both saw rents climb 1.3%, while Northern Ireland was the sole region to experience a slight decline at 0.5%.

Annual comparisons paint a similar picture of robust growth across most areas. Following London's 6% surge, the East Midlands recorded the second-highest annual increase at 4.7%, with Scotland and the North East close behind at 4.1% and 4.0% respectively. When excluding London, the national average stands at £1,170, reflecting a more modest but still significant 3.4% annual increase.

London's enduring rental market dominance

The capital's rental market continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience, with prices now £836 higher than the national average. July's 1.2% monthly increase builds on consistent growth throughout the year, reflecting sustained demand for London properties. This trend suggests tenants may need to budget carefully or consider locations slightly further from central zones to manage costs.

Industry observers note that multiple factors contribute to London's outperformance, including its employment opportunities, international appeal, and constrained housing supply. The city's rental growth has now accelerated from 5.0% in June to 6.0% in July, indicating strengthening rather than stabilising market conditions.

As rental costs continue their upward march across most of the country, tenants may wish to review their housing budgets and consider the timing of lease renewals. With London leading the charge and regional markets showing few signs of cooling, the coming months could prove challenging for those seeking affordable rental accommodation. Market analysts suggest this sustained growth reflects fundamental supply-demand imbalances rather than temporary market fluctuations.

item.title: More than 1.5m UK homes ‘unmortgageable’, claims lender
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Over 1.5 million UK properties may struggle to secure traditional mortgage financing due to characteristics that fall outside conventional lending criteria, according to new analysis from specialist lender Together. Their research suggests roughly 6% of Britain's 28 million homes could be deemed "unmortgageable" by high street banks.

What makes a property "unmortgageable"?

Mainstream lenders often reject mortgage applications for properties with unconventional features that could affect resale value or pose maintenance risks. Common red flags include:

  • Non-standard construction (e.g. concrete, timber or steel frames)
  • Thatched roofs or other unusual roofing materials
  • Flats with short leases (typically under 70 years remaining)
  • High-rise apartments above a certain floor level
  • Properties adjacent to commercial premises
  • Homes lacking basic facilities like a working kitchen or bathroom

The issue frequently emerges late in the buying process, leaving purchasers scrambling for alternative finance after a mainstream mortgage rejection.

Why buyers target unconventional properties

Despite financing challenges, many purchasers actively seek out these non-standard properties for various reasons:

  • 44% of interested buyers reported better value compared to conventional homes
  • 31% were specifically looking for renovation projects
  • 28% saw potential to add value through improvements
  • 35% of buy-to-let investors cited strong rental yield potential
  • Over a quarter were attracted by significantly lower purchase prices

However, financing remains a substantial hurdle, with 21% of buyers reporting previous mortgage rejections and 32% finding their lender options severely limited when pursuing these properties.

The specialist lending alternative

Ryan Etchells, chief commercial officer at Together, comments: "A significant portion of UK housing stock remains effectively inaccessible to ordinary buyers due to mainstream lenders' risk appetites. While these properties don't feature in official housing shortage statistics, they represent a hidden element of our supply challenges."

Specialist lenders often take a more flexible approach to property types, considering individual circumstances rather than applying rigid criteria. While interest rates may be higher than mainstream products, these options can help buyers secure properties with renovation potential or unique characteristics.

For those considering unconventional properties, researching specialist finance options early in the process could prevent transaction delays. Mortgage brokers with access to niche lenders may be particularly valuable for these purchases.
item.content:encoded:
By Bambang Setiawan

Over 1.5 million UK properties may struggle to secure traditional mortgage financing due to characteristics that fall outside conventional lending criteria, according to new analysis from specialist lender Together. Their research suggests roughly 6% of Britain's 28 million homes could be deemed "unmortgageable" by high street banks.

What makes a property "unmortgageable"?

Mainstream lenders often reject mortgage applications for properties with unconventional features that could affect resale value or pose maintenance risks. Common red flags include:

  • Non-standard construction (e.g. concrete, timber or steel frames)
  • Thatched roofs or other unusual roofing materials
  • Flats with short leases (typically under 70 years remaining)
  • High-rise apartments above a certain floor level
  • Properties adjacent to commercial premises
  • Homes lacking basic facilities like a working kitchen or bathroom

The issue frequently emerges late in the buying process, leaving purchasers scrambling for alternative finance after a mainstream mortgage rejection.

Why buyers target unconventional properties

Despite financing challenges, many purchasers actively seek out these non-standard properties for various reasons:

  • 44% of interested buyers reported better value compared to conventional homes
  • 31% were specifically looking for renovation projects
  • 28% saw potential to add value through improvements
  • 35% of buy-to-let investors cited strong rental yield potential
  • Over a quarter were attracted by significantly lower purchase prices

However, financing remains a substantial hurdle, with 21% of buyers reporting previous mortgage rejections and 32% finding their lender options severely limited when pursuing these properties.

The specialist lending alternative

Ryan Etchells, chief commercial officer at Together, comments: "A significant portion of UK housing stock remains effectively inaccessible to ordinary buyers due to mainstream lenders' risk appetites. While these properties don't feature in official housing shortage statistics, they represent a hidden element of our supply challenges."

Specialist lenders often take a more flexible approach to property types, considering individual circumstances rather than applying rigid criteria. While interest rates may be higher than mainstream products, these options can help buyers secure properties with renovation potential or unique characteristics.

For those considering unconventional properties, researching specialist finance options early in the process could prevent transaction delays. Mortgage brokers with access to niche lenders may be particularly valuable for these purchases.

item.title: Why Investors Should Build Their Funding Strategy Before Their Portfolio
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Seasoned property investors often highlight an unexpected hurdle in portfolio expansion – securing appropriate funding rather than finding suitable properties. Whilst quality investment opportunities continue to emerge in the UK market, many experienced buyers suggest that developing a robust financial strategy before property acquisition can be crucial for sustainable growth.

Funding Challenges Outweigh Property Availability

Contrary to common assumptions, the primary constraint for property investors frequently relates to financing rather than property supply. Market research indicates that whilst suitable investment properties remain available across various UK regions, lenders' increasingly cautious approach has made funding acquisition more complex. Investors might find that establishing clear financial parameters before property hunting could offer significant advantages.

Several factors contribute to these funding difficulties:

  • Tighter lending criteria following regulatory changes
  • Increased scrutiny of rental income projections
  • More stringent stress testing for portfolio landlords
  • Limited product availability for experienced investors

Strategic Financial Planning Benefits

Property investors may wish to consider developing their funding strategy as a foundational step, rather than treating it as an afterthought. This approach could potentially offer several benefits:

Improved Negotiating Position
With pre-arranged funding or clearly understood borrowing capacity, investors might find themselves in a stronger position when making offers. Sellers often favour buyers who can demonstrate financial readiness.

Faster Transaction Completion
Having financing options pre-approved could help accelerate purchase timelines, reducing the risk of missing out on time-sensitive opportunities.

Portfolio Growth Potential
A structured funding plan may allow investors to scale their portfolios more efficiently, with clear visibility on how each acquisition affects their overall borrowing capacity.

Risk Mitigation
Understanding financial limitations from the outset might help investors avoid over-leveraging or unexpected funding gaps during portfolio expansion.

Mortgage brokers specialising in investment properties often recommend that clients establish their financial parameters before commencing property searches. This might involve comprehensive affordability assessments, exploring specialist lender criteria, or considering alternative funding structures beyond traditional buy-to-let mortgages.

For those building property portfolios in today's market, prioritising financial strategy could prove as important as identifying the right properties. Whilst attractive investment opportunities continue to emerge, the ability to secure appropriate funding remains the critical factor determining long-term success for many UK property investors.

item.title: Landlord Law Blog Roundup for July
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

July saw a host of valuable updates and resources for landlords navigating the UK's complex property legislation landscape. From updated legal handbooks to monthly news roundups, property investors had several key developments to consider.

Essential Reading for Landlords

The sixth edition of the Housing Law Handbook by Diane Astin emerged as a noteworthy publication last month. This comprehensive guide provides updated coverage of crucial legislation affecting residential landlords, including recent changes to tenant rights, eviction procedures and safety regulations. Property owners might find such resources particularly valuable when reviewing their own compliance processes.

Legal handbooks can serve as practical references for both experienced landlords and those new to the buy-to-let market. With frequent legislative changes affecting the private rental sector, staying informed through authoritative sources could help landlords avoid costly compliance issues.

Monthly Legal Updates

The Landlord Law Blog maintained its regular schedule of monthly roundups, offering property investors convenient summaries of key developments. The July updates included:

  • A comprehensive June roundup covering all landlord law posts from the previous month
  • The first Newsround of July (#443), highlighting recent case law and policy changes
  • Detailed analysis of emerging trends in housing law

Such regular updates might prove especially useful for landlords managing properties across different regions of England and Wales, where local regulations can vary. Keeping abreast of these changes could help property owners adapt their practices accordingly.

For those seeking more in-depth information, the original Landlord Law Blog posts remain available online, providing full details on each development mentioned in the roundups. Property investors may wish to bookmark these resources for future reference as the regulatory landscape continues to evolve.

item.title: Section 21 ends: what possession options do landlords have now?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With the abolition of Section 21 no-fault evictions now complete, landlords in England must familiarise themselves with the new rules governing tenant possession. From 31 July 2026 onwards, property owners can no longer use the previous Section 21 procedure to regain possession of assured tenancy properties, except in limited circumstances involving tenants in a "breathing space" arrangement.

The new possession landscape under Section 8

The primary route for landlords seeking possession now involves using updated Section 8 procedures under the amended Housing Act. The system now requires landlords to use Form 3A when serving notice, with strict penalties for incorrect usage. Local authorities have been granted enhanced powers to issue civil penalty notices ranging from £7,000 up to £40,000 in certain cases.

Common pitfalls that could trigger penalties include:

  • Attempting to end tenancies via informal 'notice to quit' letters
  • Verbal requests for tenants to vacate the property
  • Using outdated Section 21 notices (now invalid)
  • Relying on possession grounds without reasonable belief in their validity
  • Re-letting within 12 months after using no-fault grounds

Available grounds for possession

The Renters Rights Act 2025 introduced significant changes to Schedule 2 of the Housing Act, creating a revised framework of possession grounds. These fall into two categories:

  • Mandatory grounds - Where courts must grant possession if evidence satisfies the specified criteria
  • Discretionary grounds - Where judges have flexibility in deciding whether to grant possession orders

Contrary to popular belief, two no-fault grounds remain available to landlords:

  • Ground 1 - When the property is needed for the landlord or their immediate family to live in
  • Ground 1A - When vacant possession is required to sell the property

Both grounds come with important restrictions, including a 12-month prohibited period during which possession cannot be sought. Landlords should note that using these grounds then re-letting the property within a year could result in substantial £40,000 penalties.

As the private rental sector adapts to these changes, landlords may wish to review their procedures and seek professional advice to ensure compliance with the new regulations. The shift emphasises the importance of proper documentation and valid reasons when seeking possession, marking a significant change in landlord-tenant relationships in England.
